en: Varoufakis insists that the difference between rent and profit is not a “calculation” (what is left after costs), but a qualitative difference tied to the mode of acquisition, since profit is structurally vulnerable to market competition, whereas rent is anchored in a position of control and tends not to be eroded by competition in the same way. In the author's words: “En el feudalismo, la renta era bastante fácil de entender. Gracias a un accidente de nacimiento, o a un decreto real, el señor feudal obtenía las escrituras de una parcela que le daban poder para extraer parte de la cosecha producida por los campesinos que habían nacido y crecido en esa tierra. En el capitalismo, entender el significado de la renta y distinguirla del beneficio es mucho más complejo; se trata de una dificultad de la que fui testigo directo cuando era profesor universitario y me esforzaba por ayudar a mis alumnos a distinguir ambas cosas. No existe una diferencia aritmética: tanto la renta como el beneficio son el dinero que queda una vez que se han pagado los costes. La diferencia es más sutil, cualitativa, casi abstracta: el beneficio es vulnerable a la competencia de mercado, y la renta no lo es. El motivo estriba en sus diferentes orígenes. La renta deriva del acceso privilegiado a bienes cuya oferta es rígida, como el suelo fértil o las tierras que contienen combustibles fósiles; no se pueden producir más recursos de este tipo, por mucho dinero que se invierta. El beneficio, por el contrario, acaba en los bolsillos de los empresarios que han invertido en cosas que de otro modo no existirían —por ejemplo, la bombilla de Edison o el iPhone de Jobs—. El hecho de que estas mercancías hayan sido inventadas y creadas por alguien, y de que, por lo tanto, otra persona pueda inventar y crear una versión mejor, es lo que hace que el beneficio sea vulnerable a la competencia.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 106- 107)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis makes explicit the sociological nuance of the argument by separating the cultural status of profit (beneficio) from its systemic status as the effective engine of accumulation, although profit remains as aspirational language (“ambición”, “objetivo”, “aspiración”), but the central gear can operate decoupled from profits, allowing the elite to treat profit as a contingency and shift the center of gravity toward other sources of power and extraction. The author connects the “optionality” of profit to the shift in the system's fuel: “Luego, por primera vez desde que el capitalismo se había despertado dos siglos y medio antes, el beneficio dejó de ser el combustible que encendía el motor de la economía mundial, impulsando la inversión y la innovación. Ese papel, el de alimentar la economía, lo asumió el dinero de los bancos centrales.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 92)</2>. At this point, the author directly formulates the decoupling: “El beneficio siguió siendo la ambición de todo capitalista, el objetivo de cualquier vendedor, la aspiración de las personas que luchaban por una vida más cómoda. Pero la acumulación de capital, el proceso que crea riqueza aumentando el tamaño del pastel, se desvinculó de los beneficios, al igual que el final del sistema de Bretton Woods y el posterior auge del Minotauro habían disociado el trabajo duro de la mejora de las condiciones de vida. La intención de los banqueros centrales no era sustituir los beneficios. Simplemente cayeron en una trampa que ellos mismos habían creado. El pánico de 2008 había acabado con la demanda de dinero para inversiones, causando una sobreoferta que deprimió los tipos de interés. Cuanto más caían éstos, mayor era la convicción de los inversores de que las cosas estaban tan mal que sería una locura invertir. Sin embargo, se siguieron inyectando billones de dólares procedentes de los bancos centrales en las finanzas, de modo que el círculo vicioso continuó, con los tipos de interés bajando cada vez más: hasta cero o incluso cifras negativas. Cuando los conglomerados y los gobiernos empezaron a depender de los préstamos sin intereses, y las empresas de los países en desarrollo pedían prestado más que sus gobiernos —más de 2 billones de dólares a finales de la década de 2010—, los banqueros centrales se enfrentaron a un feo dilema: o bien cerrar el grifo del dinero, lo que significaría hacer saltar por los aires el capitalismo financiarizado tras haber impreso mucho dinero para salvarlo, o bien seguir inyectando dinero en el sistema, esperando que sucediera un milagro pero, en realidad, facilitando la sustitución del beneficio como motivación y lubricante del capitalismo. Como era de esperar, optaron por lo segundo. La angustia de los bancos centrales fue la alegría de los nubelistas. En este período, empresarios intrépidos y talentosos como Jeff Bezos y Elon Musk pudieron construir su capital en la nube, supercaro y ultrapoderoso, sin necesidad de hacer ninguna de las tres cosas que los capitalistas habían hecho tradicionalmente para expandirse: pedir dinero prestado a algún banco, vender grandes partes de su negocio a otros o generar grandes beneficios para pagar nuevo capital social.” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 93)</4>. Varoufakis uses the metaphor of the “global Minotaur” to name the macroeconomic arrangement that succeeds Bretton Woods, in which the US trade deficit and the return of financial surpluses to Wall Street function as a mechanism for the “recycling” of capital and for the stabilization of the system, shifting the axis of economic dynamics to the financial-monetary sphere <5>Varoufakis</5><6>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 43-46)</6>. In an illustrative register of the same phenomenon, Varoufakis points out that agents were able to pursue dominance without immediate profitability, summarizing the idea of the irrelevance of profit in the face of the capture of position: “Ambos sabían que el beneficio era irrelevante. Lo importante era aprovechar la oportunidad de establecer un dominio total del mercado. En 2021, Goldman Sachs, uno de los bancos menos amables de Wall Street, asombró al mundo financiero al publicar un ‘índice de tecnologías no rentables’, que demuestra perfectamente cómo el capitalismo se ha emancipado de los beneficios […].” <7>Varoufakis</7><8>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 94)</8>. <9>↩</9>

In a historical key, Varoufakis anchors this inversion in a long construction. Capitalism would have emerged when profit replaced rent as the driving force, and technofeudalism would mark the return of rent to the center, now reconfigured by the cloud. This makes it possible to explain why the lexicon of “profit” does not always describe the phenomenon well, since the central mechanism comes close to toll rent, extracted through the administration of economic and social traffic within private environments. <1>↩</1>

In this thesis, the expression “nuvistas” (cloudalists) is employed as an operational translation of the category formulated by Varoufakis to designate the holders of cloud capital, that is, the agents who control digital infrastructures of access, circulation and extraction. The terminological choice seeks to preserve the conceptual image of the cloud without multiplying competing translations throughout the text. <1>↩</1>

Varoufakis uses the term nubelistas to name the new technofeudal elite and to mark that this is not merely a matter of “digital entrepreneurs”, but of a fraction that reaches a level of power capable of displacing the top of the social hierarchy. The author formulates this directly when he states that “Como resultado, sus propietarios —los nubelistas— han adquirido la habilidad de hacer algo que los Edison, los Westinghouse y los Ford nunca lograron: convertirse en una clase revolucionaria que desplaza activamente a los capitalistas de lo más alto del orden jerárquico de la sociedad.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 85)</2>. This displacement is not presented as mere business superiority, but as a reconfiguration of the objective and of the mechanism of economic power: even though they invest heavily in R&D, politics, marketing and even strategies of cartelization and union dismantling, the nubelistas “no lo hacen para vender mercancías con el máximo beneficio posible, sino para extraer las máximas rentas de los capitalistas que sí lo hacen.” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 115)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Varoufakis <1>(2024, p. 7-8)</1> describes the hierarchical reordering produced by the cloud as a relationship of dependence: the holders of “traditional” capital cease to command the center of the system and come to operate under the power of the new elite, by becoming vassals (vasallos) of the owners of cloud capital (capital en la nube). This vassalage is not merely nominal: it translates into governance and dependence on the channel, insofar as “los fabricantes capitalistas convencionales se ven obligados […] a vender sus bienes según el dictamen de los ‘nubelistas’, a pagarles una tasa por el privilegio”, in a relationship that “no difiere” from the one “los vasallos con sus señores feudales” had <2>Varoufakis</2><3>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 81)</3>. In terms of systematization, the author further frames the arrangement as a “sistema de clases tecnofeudal”, in which the nubelistas become a new ruling class and reduce “al resto de los capitalistas […] a un estatus de vasallaje” <4>Varoufakis</4><5>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 201)</5>. <6>↩</6>

Varoufakis describes the social effect of the power of the nubelistas as a reorganization of classes typical of technofeudalism, in which conventional capitalists come to sell under the dictate of the cloud and to pay for the “privilege” of access, in a relationship analogous to that of the vasallos with their señores feudales, while the rest are pushed into forms of functional servitude tied to the platform. In an exemplifying key, Varoufakis explicitly brings the structure of Amazon close to this same regime of concession, charging and automated discipline: “La relación de Jeff con los vendedores de amazon.com no es muy distinta. Les concede feudos digitales basados en la nube, a cambio de una cuota, y luego deja que su ‘algo-sheriff’ vigile y cobre.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 78)</2>. The author frames this shift as part of the “verdadera disrupción histórica” linked to the automation of the power of command and to the mass conversion of subjects into cloud serfs: “No, la verdadera disrupción histórica fue automatizar el poder para mandar del capital y cedérselo a gente que estaba ‘fuera’ de la fábrica, la tienda o la oficina: convertirnos a todos, a los proletarios de la nube y a los demás, en siervos de la nube al servicio directo (no remunerado) del capital en la nube, sin la mediación de ningún mercado.” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 80)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Riot defines virtual content as a “personal right” and records that the license is revocable, that is, the consumer does not acquire a good by transfer but receives a conditional grant. It then closes the door on ownership by stating that the user “will have no property right or other kind of right over their account” and that “all rights to your account are and will always be the property of Riot Games and will revert to its benefit”. The choice of language matters because it shifts the relationship into a regime in which permanence and collection are not legally stabilized positions, but effects of a tolerated access. <1>↩</1>

The developer describes Virtual Content as a personal right granted by license and insists that it “has no monetary value”, in addition to preventing its transfer or conversion into “real world” money, which legally drains the idea of an estate accumulated within the fief <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. The discursive engineering here is simple and brutal. If what is inside the account is declared “without value”, then the loss of the collection tends to be presented as a natural effect of the termination of the relationship, and not as the suppression of an economically relevant position. <3>↩</3>

The Terms of Service establish the company's prerogative to terminate or suspend the account if it is “reasonably determined” that a violation has occurred, and include among the grounds what it describes as the “best interest of our community or of the Services”, terms that function as internal governance criteria and not as public standards of adversarial hearing or proportionality <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. The consequence is that the fief does not need to justify “just cause” in an external sense. It is enough to fit the conduct into a repertoire that the fief itself writes and applies, and that it can modify on its own at any time without prior notice to the user. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis recognizes the appearance of continuity. The nubelistas may seem like “capitalists on steroids” because they invested heavily and built their technological power, but the author fixes the final distinction in purpose, according to which the investment does not aim to compete in capitalist markets, but rather to make the market dispensable, replacing it with private domains of access and rentier extraction. He makes the appearance of continuity explicit when he states: “Es cierto, papá, que los nubelistas son —o al menos eran— capitalistas con esteroides [...] los nubelistas tuvieron que crearlo desde cero [...] invirtieron gigantescas cantidades de dinero en tecnología.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 113)</2>. He then shifts the focus of the investment to the object and to the purpose: “una mercancía es un bien o un servicio que se produce para ser vendido y obtener un beneficio. Los resultados de una búsqueda no se generan para ser vendidos. Alexa y Siri no responden a nuestras preguntas a cambio de dinero [...] su objetivo es muy distinto: captar y modificar nuestra atención.” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 113)</4>. Even when there is payment, the function remains the same: “Estos aparatos se alquilan o venden a un precio barato, no por el beneficio insignificante (a menudo negativo) que se obtiene de ellos, sino para acceder a nuestros hogares y, a través de ellos, a una parte cada vez mayor de nuestra atención.” <5>Varoufakis</5><6>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 113)</6>. It is this infrastructural power over attention that makes extraction from third parties possible: “Es este poder sobre nuestra atención el que les permite cobrar la renta de la nube a los capitalistas vasallos que se dedican al anticuado negocio de vender sus mercancías.” <7>Varoufakis</7><8>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 113)</8>. The conclusion closes the criterion of distinction with the formulation you have already selected: “En última instancia, la inversión de los nubelistas no se destina a competir dentro de mercados capitalistas, sino a conseguir que los abandonemos por completo.” <9>Varoufakis</9><10>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 113)</10>. <11>↩</11>

Varoufakis insists that the “cloud” is not immateriality, but a planetary physical infrastructure, composed of data warehouses, rows of servers and a mesh of connections that makes continuous capture and processing possible. In the author's words: “Sin duda, no es menos físico que esos otros tipos de capital, porque la metáfora de la nube es sólo eso: una metáfora. En realidad, la nube está formada por grandes almacenes de datos que contienen filas interminables de servidores conectados por una red de sensores y cables que se extiende por todo el planeta.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 71-72)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Here Varoufakis offers a technical-material definition of <1>capital en la nube</1>, insisting that it combines a physical base and an architecture of control, integrating networked machinery, communications hardware and the algorithmic layer that makes it possible to automate coordination and modulate behavior. In the author's words: “El capital en la nube se define, físicamente, como la acumulación de maquinaria conectada en red, software, algoritmos basados en IA y hardware de comunicaciones que recorren todo el planeta y realizan una amplia variedad de tareas, nuevas y antiguas, por ejemplo: incitar a miles de millones de personas no asalariadas (siervos de la nube) a trabajar gratis (y a menudo de manera inconsciente) para reponer el stock de capital en la nube (por ejemplo, subir fotos y vídeos a Instagram o TikTok, o colgar críticas de películas, restaurantes y libros).” <2>Varoufakis</2><3>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 196)</3>. <4>↩</4>

Varoufakis marks the singularity of “cloud capital” by stating that it dispenses with reproduction via classic wage labor, insofar as it replenishes itself through the imposition of free contributions on a civilizational scale. “He aquí un atisbo de la razón por la cual el capital en la nube es tan fundamentalmente nuevo, diferente y aterrador: hasta ahora, el capital se ha reproducido dentro de un mercado laboral, como la fábrica, la oficina o el almacén. Eran los trabajadores asalariados quienes, con la ayuda de máquinas, producían los bienes que se vendían para generar beneficios, que a su vez financiaban sus salarios y la producción de más máquinas: así es cómo se acumulaba y reproducía el capital. El capital en la nube, en cambio, puede reproducirse sin mano de obra asalariada. ¿Cómo? Imponiendo a casi toda la humanidad que contribuya a su reproducción, ¡gratis!” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 72)</2>. <3>↩</3>

The author then broadens the argument by suggesting that it is not only “content” that is extracted, but the very capacity to govern conduct, since the free contribution of users feeds behavior patterns that, when captured and processed, reinforce the power of command of cloud capital over choices, attention and trajectories. In the author's words: “Cada vez que nos conectamos para disfrutar de los servicios de estos algoritmos, no nos queda más opción que hacer un pacto fáustico con sus propietarios. Para utilizar los servicios personalizados que ofrecen sus algoritmos, debemos someternos a un modelo de negocio basado en la recopilación de nuestros datos, el seguimiento de nuestra actividad y la selección invisible de nuestros contenidos. Una vez que lo hacemos, el algoritmo se dedica a vendernos cosas mientras vende nuestra atención a terceros. En ese punto, sucede algo más profundo que da a sus propietarios un poder inmenso: predecir nuestro comportamiento, guiar nuestras preferencias, influir en nuestras decisiones, hacernos cambiar de opinión para, así, reducirnos a sus sirvientes no remunerados, cuyo trabajo es proporcionar nuestra información, nuestra atención, nuestra identidad y, sobre todo, los patrones de comportamiento que entrenan a sus algoritmos.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 71)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis treats Amazon as an empirical demonstration that the platform is not “a digital market”, but a private domain whose logic already operates outside market capitalism, even though purchases and sales take place there. In the author's words: “‘Entra en amazon.com y habrás salido del capitalismo. A pesar de todo lo que se compra y se vende ahí, has entrado en un mundo que no puede considerarse un mercado, ni siquiera uno digital.’ Cuando digo esto a la gente, y lo hago a menudo en conferencias y debates, me miran como si estivesse loco.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 77)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis uses Alexa to make the existential dimension of the technofief tangible: the device is only a minimal piece of a cloud-based network of power, in which the user becomes a subordinate node, with little or no understanding of or control over the forces that govern them. In the author's words: “un minúsculo engranaje en una vasta red de poder basada en la nube, en la que tú eres un mero nodo, una mota de polvo digital, en el mejor de los casos, un juguete para unas fuerzas que escapan a tu comprensión o control.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 60)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis uses the Google ecosystem to show how the technofief consolidates itself through the infrastructure of operating system and store, transforming external production into dependence on the channel and allowing recurring extraction through access/distribution. In the author's words: “Android no era ni mejor ni peor que el sistema operativo que Sony, Blackberry, Nokia y otros habían —o podrían haber— desarrollado por su cuenta. Pero tenía un superpoder: el abundante capital en la nube de Google, que actuó como un imán para los desarrolladores externos que Sony, Blackberry y Nokia nunca podrían haber atraído por sí solos. ¿Cómo iban éstos a resistirse? Aunque de mala gana, se vieron obligados a aceptar el papel de fabricante de teléfonos capitalista y vasallo, que subsistía con las sobras de los beneficios por la venta de su hardware, mientras Google se embolsaba la renta de la nube producida por otra multitud de emprendedores y capitalistas vasallos: los desarrolladores externos que ahora producían aplicaciones a la venta en Google Play. Así es como Google creó Google Play, la única alternativa seria a Apple Store.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 110)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis formulates the surveillance arm of cloud capital as an asymmetry of knowledge, through which Apple and Google come to know more than the user about their consumption, reading, movements and encounters — and this is power, because it sustains prediction, targeting and monetization of conduct. “Aun así, resulta increíble que nuestra identidad digital no sea nuestra ni del Estado. Dispersada por innumerables mundos digitales de propiedad privada, tiene muchos dueños, ninguno de los cuales somos nosotros: un banco privado posee tus códigos de identificación y todo tu historial de compras. Facebook está íntimamente familiarizado con quién —y qué— te gusta. X recuerda cada pequeña idea que ha llamado tu atención, cada opinión con la que estuviste de acuerdo y aquella que te enfureció y con la que te entretuviste distraídamente antes de seguir leyendo la cronología. Apple y Google saben mejor que tú lo que ves, lees, compras, con quién te reúnes, cuándo y dónde.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 66-67)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis uses the Huawei/Android case to show that technofeudal infrastructure is also a geopolitical instrument: controlling operating systems and usage permissions becomes a state weapon in the dispute for technological hegemony, redrawing the “cold war” in a digital key. In the author's words: “El 15 de mayo de 2019, el presidente Donald Trump promulgó un decreto que, a efectos prácticos, prohibía a Google que permitiera el uso de su sistema operativo Android en smartphones fabricados por Huawei, la empresa china de telecomunicaciones. En la práctica, Trump estaba expulsando a Huawei del feudo en la nube de Google, cuya escala es global. Washington también le dijo a los gobiernos europeos que suspendieran el plan que implicaba a Huawei en el despliegue de redes móviles 5G en Europa. Aquello era mucho más que una locura trumpista.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 126)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis uses the example of TikTok to show that the “rivalry” between platforms does not function as market competition, based on price and quality, but as a dispute between fiefs for attention and user migration, which ends up creating another territory for the same serfs, offering a different experience within the same logic. “El hecho de que TikTok haya robado con éxito la atención de los usuarios de otras redes sociales no se debe a que ofrezca precios más baratos o a que la calidad de las ‘amistades’ o las relaciones que facilita sea mejor. TikTok creó un nuevo feudo en la nube para siervos de la nube que buscaban una experiencia online diferente a la que migrar.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 115)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis stresses that the category “capitalist vassal” is not synonymous with small producer, since it includes everyone from artisans to large manufacturers. The unifying criterion is structural dependence on the channel. Selling comes to mean selling through a platform and, for this reason, a relevant part of the net income of these agents is appropriated by the nubelistas as extraction of cloud rent. “De hecho, no todos los capitalistas vasallos son pequeños artesanos, algunos son grandes fabricantes capitalistas. Pero grandes o pequeños, poderosos o no, todos los capitalistas vasallos, por definición, dependen en mayor o menor medida de la venta de sus mercancías a través de un sitio de comercio electrónico, ya sea Amazon, eBay o Alibaba, y una parte considerable de sus ingresos netos se la llevan los nubelistas de los que dependen” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 111)</2>. This formulation ties together, at the same time, the heterogeneity of the group and the decisive point of the technofief: the size of the producer does not matter, proprietary mediation concentrates the gateway to consumption and converts “selling” into paying a toll to exist in the digital territory. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis describes the discipline of the technofief as a power of exclusion that operates through permanent vulnerability, insofar as the capitalist vassal does not need to be coerced by physical violence, because it is enough for the platform to cut a link (a <1>link</1>, an access, an indexing) for them to lose clientele and literally “disappear” from the online world. It is this constant, impersonal and automatable threat that functions as a technique of government and sustains what he calls “tecnoterror aséptico” (aseptic technoterror). In the author's words: “Todo capitalista vasallo sabe que si se elimina un enlace de su sitio en la nube podría perder el acceso a la mayor parte de sus clientes. Y con la eliminación de uno o dos enlaces del motor de búsqueda de Google o de un par de páginas de comercio electrónico y redes sociales, podrían desaparecer por completo del mundo online. El tecnofeudalismo se fundamenta en un tecnoterror aséptico” <2>Varoufakis</2><3>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 112)</3>. As a comparative frame, Varoufakis opens the paragraph by contrasting “classic” feudal collection (physical coercion) with the fact that the nubelistas “clássica”: discipline is now exercised through architecture of access, ranking and intermediation, and not through direct force <4>Varoufakis</4><5>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 119)</5>. <6>↩</6>

Varoufakis deliberately resorts to the language of servitude to mark that the user's everyday participation is neither neutral nor merely “consumption”, but a form of structural contribution to the wealth and power of the new ruling class, via unpaid labor. In the preface, the author closes the diagnosis of class reordering with a direct passage in which, after asserting the vassalage of “traditional” capital, he concludes: “En cuanto al resto, hemos vuelto a nuestra antigua condición de siervos y contribuimos a la riqueza y el poder de la nueva clase dominante con nuestro trabajo no remunerado, además de, cuando tenemos la oportunidad, con el trabajo asalariado que realizamos.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 8)</2>. In a register of systematization, the appendix consolidates this conversion into a rule of class structure by describing that “casi todo el mundo actúa como un siervo de la nube [...], contribuyendo a que el capital en la nube acumule y construya los feudos en la nube [...] que están sustituyendo a los mercados.” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 201)</4>. Besides speaking of a “return” to servitude as an interpretive key to technofeudalism, Varoufakis explicitly names the contemporary condition as siervos de la nube and links it directly to the reproduction of capital en la nube through free labor, shifting the axis of exploitation outside classic wage employment. At the close of the section devoted to this social figure, he formulates the thesis in unequivocal terms: “La verdadera revolución que ha impuesto a la humanidad es la conversión de miles de millones de personas en siervos de la nube dispuestos a trabajar gratis para reproducir el capital en la nube en beneficio de sus propietarios.” <5>Varoufakis</5><6>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 76)</6>. This naming gains weight when the author makes explicit that the decisive trait is not the voluntariness of the engagement, but the fact that it is converted into unpaid manufacturing that feeds accumulation: “Lo mismo sucede con los miles de millones de nosotros que producimos involuntariamente capital en la nube. El hecho de que lo hagamos de manera voluntaria, incluso con gusto, no quita que seamos fabricantes no remunerados; siervos de la nube cuyo duro trabajo cotidiano, fruto de su iniciativa, enriquece a un pequeño grupo de multimilmillonarios” <7>Varoufakis</7><8>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 76)</8>. <9>↩</9>

Varoufakis coins “cloud proletarians” (“proletarios de la nube”) to name wage workers whose exploitation intensifies because command over the labor process comes to be exercised by cloud-based algorithms, capable of imposing rhythms and targets that push the body “physically to the limit”. He emphasizes, at the same time, the historical continuity of suffering: despite technological change (from gears and belts to connected algorithmic systems), the experience of wear would be immediately recognizable to proletarians of earlier generations. In the author's words: “La forma en que los proletarios de la nube —el término con el que me refiero a los trabajadores asalariados a los que algoritmos basados en la nube llevan físicamente al límite— sufren en el trabajo sería reconocida al instante por generaciones enteras de proletarios anteriores” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 73)</2>. As a frame, he anticipates the objection “does this matter?” and answers that the exchange of the control mechanism (gears vs. algorithms connected to the “red neuronal de la empresa”) does not alter the essential: what changes is the instrument of command, not the fact of imposed exhaustion <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 73)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Varoufakis shows that the gig economy is not merely a “new service sector” within the market, but a direct coupling to the technofief, where platforms erect digital territories (cloud fiefs) and connect to them task workers (drivers, couriers, various providers) not to pay wages and extract competitive profit, but to tax access and appropriate a stable portion of these workers' income. The typical form of this capture is the standardized commission on individual earnings, which he explicitly names as cloud rent, that is, a recurring toll charged for intermediation and for control of the channel. In the author's words: “conectaron sus feudos en la nube a una gran variedad de […] trabajadores a destajo […] a los que cobraban una comisión fija de sus ingresos. Una renta de la nube” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 111)</2>. Conceptually, the technofief does not need to “employ” in the classic sense: it administers entry and visibility (access to <3>clients</3>) and, for this reason, manages to convert precarious labor into a permanent source of rent, shifting the center of gravity of accumulation from profit to the platform toll. <4>↩</4>

Varoufakis describes the algorithm-bosses (algo-jefes) as a qualitative mutation of precarization because command over labor no longer depends on human mediation and operates instead as automatic discipline, without the brakes of empathy, negotiation or explanation. The worker is governed by a “non-corporeal” entity that assigns tasks, measures times and adjusts the pace in real time; precisely because it carries no moral limits (not even the “hypocrisy” of humans), the algorithm can cut paid hours, accelerate cadences to exhaustion and dismiss for “inefficiency” as a routine procedure. “Liberados de los escrúpulos que tienen hasta los seres humanos inhumanos, los ‘algo-jefes’ son libres de reducir las horas pagadas a los trabajadores, aumentar su ritmo hasta niveles de locura o echarlos a la calle por ‘ineficientes’” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 74)</2>. The disciplinary effect culminates in the experience of helplessness: the person dismissed by the system falls into a “Kafkaesque spiral”, unable to speak with anyone who might explain or allow contestation, which reinforces technofeudal power through the permanent fear of exclusion <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 74)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Varoufakis anticipates a directly anti-union impact of algorithmic command by suggesting that the same computational capacity used to solve complex problems can be redirected to the logistical engineering of exploitation, making collective organization a technical target. He builds the hypothesis by analogy, observing that algorithms already “mapean” and “diseñan” solutions without human intervention in domains such as the discovery of antibiotics and then asks what would prevent a similar algorithm from “diseñar una cadena de suministro global que evite los almacenes o las fábricas en las que los sindicatos tienen posibilidades de organizar a los trabajadores”. The consequence is formulated in a direct and extreme manner, as a plausible horizon of the technofief, when he concludes that “Los sindicatos podrían desaparecer, e incluso no llegar a formarse.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 74)</2>. <3>↩</3>

This is a reference to the imaginary of the German-language author Franz Kafka, especially the novels <1>O Processo</1> (1925) and <2>O Castelo</2> (1926). The expression is interpreted as a cultural shortcut for describing an environment of impersonal authority, with decisions lacking intelligible justification, labyrinthine rules and the frustration of subjects who try to appeal to bodies that cannot be reached, or that simply do not exist as a responsible interlocutor. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis also identifies an architectural obstacle to collective mobilization. Cloud domination is experienced in an atomized way, through individualized mediations, so that political coordination faces not only repression or economic asymmetry, but the practical erosion of the encounter between people subjected to similar conditions. For this thesis, the point is less the political strategy for overcoming technofeudalism and more the perception that the infrastructure that organizes access and enjoyment also organizes isolation, comparison, dispersion and difficulty of collective contestation. In this register, Varoufakis states that “El tecnofeudalismo levanta una nueva gran barrera que impide la movilización contra él” and then names the core of this barrier as the material separation between the two poles of exploitation in the cloud: “La nueva gran barrera es el aislamiento físico entre los siervos de la nube y los proletarios de la nube.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 176)</2>. The form of this isolation is described as permanent mediation by devices and screens, since “Interactuamos con el capital en la nube, y estamos sometidos a él, a través de nuestras pantallas personales, nuestros teléfonos móviles, los dispositivos digitales que supervisan y controlan a los trabajadores de los almacenes de Amazon”, which produces a direct consequence for collective action, because “La acción colectiva es más difícil cuando las personas tienen menos oportunidades de reunirse.” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 176)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Varoufakis describes the discipline of the technofief as a power of exclusion that operates through permanent vulnerability, insofar as the capitalist vassal does not need to be coerced by physical violence, because it is enough for the platform to cut a link (a <1>link</1>, an access, an indexing) for them to lose clientele and literally “disappear” from the online world. It is this constant, impersonal and automatable threat that functions as a technique of government and sustains what he calls “tecnoterror aséptico” (aseptic technoterror). In the author's words: “Todo capitalista vasallo sabe que si se elimina un enlace de su sitio en la nube podría perder el acceso a la mayor parte de sus clientes. Y con la eliminación de uno o dos enlaces del motor de búsqueda de Google o de un par de páginas de comercio electrónico y redes sociales, podrían desaparecer por completo del mundo online. El tecnofeudalismo se fundamenta en un tecnoterror aséptico” <2>Varoufakis</2><3>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 112)</3>. As a comparative frame, Varoufakis opens the paragraph by contrasting “classic” feudal collection (physical coercion) with the fact that the nubelistas “no necesitan alguaciles para confiscar o desalojar”: discipline is now exercised through architecture of access, ranking and intermediation, and not through direct force <4>Varoufakis</4><5>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 119)</5>. <6>↩</6>

Varoufakis describes the algorithm-bosses (algo-jefes) as a qualitative mutation of precarization because command over labor no longer depends on human mediation and operates instead as automatic discipline, without the brakes of empathy, negotiation or explanation. The worker is governed by a “non-corporeal” entity that assigns tasks, measures times and adjusts the pace in real time; precisely because it carries no moral limits (not even the “hypocrisy” of humans), the algorithm can cut paid hours, accelerate cadences to exhaustion and dismiss for “inefficiency” as a routine procedure. “Liberados de los escrúpulos que tienen hasta los seres humanos inhumanos, los ‘algo-jefes’ son libres de reducir las horas pagadas a los trabajadores, aumentar su ritmo hasta niveles de locura o echarlos a la calle por ‘ineficientes’” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 74)</2>. The disciplinary effect culminates in the experience of helplessness: the person dismissed by the system falls into a “Kafkaesque spiral”, unable to speak with anyone who might explain or allow contestation, which reinforces technofeudal power through the permanent fear of exclusion <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 74)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Varoufakis introduces a strategic nuance by insisting that the same architecture that erects isolation also carries a possibility of use as a political response. In the same movement in which he describes the “new great barrier” as “el aislamiento físico entre los siervos de la nube y los proletarios de la nube”, he stresses that this continuous mediation by screens and devices not only hinders traditional gathering and coordination, but also offers a technical means of collective recomposition. That is why, right after stating that “La acción colectiva es más difícil cuando las personas tienen menos oportunidades de reunirse”, Varoufakis concludes that precisely there lies an unexpected power, since cloud capital “confiere a los potenciales rebeldes […] la capacidad de crear coaliciones, organizarse y actuar a través de la nube.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 176)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis concludes that, in the face of the fragmentation and isolation produced by technofeudalism, effective resistance requires a broader social composition than the classic form of mobilization. The argument is formulated as a strategic requirement to bring together subjects who, in the current arrangement, appear separated by different positions and functions in the cloud, since “para tener alguna posibilidad de derrocar al tecnofeudalismo y de que el demos vuelva a la democracia, es necesario reunir no sólo al proletariado tradicional y al de la nube, sino a los siervos de la nube y, además, al menos a algunos capitalistas vasallos”, because “únicamente una gran coalición que los incluya a todos puede debilitar lo bastante el tecnofeudalismo.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 175)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis shifts the value of cloud capital to the everyday production of users, maintaining that the physical infrastructure would lack value without the content and digital traces supplied for free on a civilizational scale. This condition of cloud serfdom does not operate merely as diffuse economic extraction, but as an attentional and behavioral captivity: permanent engagement with smartphones and tablets is the means by which ordinary life is converted into unpaid manufacturing of the capital stock that sustains the “new lords”. In the author's words: “La parte más valiosa del stock del capital en la nube no son sus componentes físicos, sino las historias publicadas en Facebook, los vídeos subidos a TikTok y YouTube, las fotos de Instagram, los chistes y los insultos en X, las reseñas de Amazon o incluso nuestros desplazamientos [...] El capital en la nube puede reproducirse sin mano de obra asalariada. ¿Cómo? Imponiendo a casi toda la humanidad que contribuya a su reproducción, ¡gratis!” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 72-75)</2>. The consequence is that technical-scientific advances culminate in a regime of practical governance of attention and conduct, since cloud capital: “ha descompuesto al individuo en fragmentos de datos, una identidad compuesta de elecciones expresadas por clics que sus algoritmos son capaces de manipular [...] para que todos nosotros nos convirtamos en siervos de la nube, pegados a nuestros smartphones y nuestras tabletas, produciendo ansiosamente el capital en la nube que mantiene a nuestros ‘nuevos señores’ en las nubes.” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 15; 79)</4>. For the author, the “true revolution” of the system is precisely this conversion of billions of people into voluntary and unpaid manufacturers of algorithmic power <5>Varoufakis</5><6>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 76)</6>. <7>↩</7>

Varoufakis describes technofeudal dependence as a captivity of data and social life, in which the platform creates exit costs by capturing what gives practical continuity to the user's digital identity, so that to “migrate” is not to change a service, but to lose an organized part of one's own online life. That is why, when addressing the asymmetry of power between platform and user, he observes that corporations “pueden tratar a sus usuarios como quieran” and asks when was the last time anyone refused the terms of an update, precisely because “tienen varios rehenes: nuestros contactos, amigos, historiales de chat, fotos, música, vídeos, todo lo cual perderemos si nos pasamos a un feudo en la nube de la competencia” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 155)</2>. The structural consequence is that domination does not depend only on the price or quality of the service, but on private ownership of the networks and archives that stabilize sociability and digital memory, converting the very possibility of exit into a threat of existential discontinuity and reinforcing the “fief” nature of these infrastructures. <3>↩</3>

For Marx <1>([2013])</1>, the passage from manufacture to large-scale industry reorganizes the subordination of labor as a systemic effect of machinery and of the factory regime. Discipline no longer depends only on immediate personal command, but on the objective form of the productive process and its internal administration. That is why, in describing the factory, Marx <2>([2013], p. 608-609)</2> observes that technical subordination to the “uniform motion” of the instrument of labor “creates a barrack-like discipline, which develops into a complete factory regime”, with its own supervision and hierarchization. In this same key, the internal normativity of the establishment appears as a kind of private juridicity of capital: “in place of the whip”, there arises the “factory supervisor's book of penalties”, that is, a regular device of command and sanction that stabilizes employer power as government of time and of the body within the productive unit. The point that matters to the argument is that, in Marx, subordination becomes legible as a form of the process: it materializes in machinery, in rhythm and in the discipline immanent to the factory system, which converts technical coordination into social command. It is precisely this intuition (command as material organization of the conditions of activity) that Varoufakis <3>(2024, p. 80-81)</3> moves outside the factory when he describes “cloud capital” as an infrastructure of extraction based on mediation and modification of behavior. When he states that cloud capital “automatizó […] el poder para mandar” and “transferió a los ‘algos’”, the author is naming a mutation in which the classic functions of command (over labor and consumption) cease to depend on the delimited productive space and come to operate, continuously, through digital architectures that govern flows of visibility, relevance and engagement. Hence the decisive formula for its fit with the notion of diffuse capture: “convertirnos […] en ‘siervos de la nube’”, providing “no remunerado” service to cloud capital, “sin la mediación de ningún mercado”. The “historical disruption”, therefore, is not merely the automation of tasks, but the automation of command and its redistribution through algorithmic devices that operate in ordinary everyday life. Not by chance, Varoufakis makes explicit that, by providing content and interactions, “somos nosotros quienes producimos y reproducimos […] el stock del capital en la nube”, even if voluntarily and pleasurably; and defines the “third nature” of this capital as “un medio producido de modificación del comportamiento”, capable of ordering consumers and converting social participation into reproduction of the cloud capital stock itself <4>Varoufakis</4><5>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 75-76)</5>. It is the passage from disciplinary command concentrated in the factory regime to infrastructural command distributed through algorithmic mediations that sustains, in the body of the work, the idea that subordination can operate as diffuse capture of social activity, converting attention, time and behavior into continuous economic input: the platform does not “compel” through classic coercion, but governs the material and semiotic conditions under which action becomes capable of conversion into value. <6>↩</6>

Varoufakis maintains that the classic political base of social democracy comes undone when the union counterweight ceases to operate as a credible threat against the new elite, since the architecture of labor under the cloud fragments and weakens the capacity for collective organization. He formulates the change in historical contrast, recalling that “Antaño, los socialdemócratas tenían cierto poder sobre los industriales porque contaban con el respaldo de los sindicatos y podían amenazar con una regulación adversa”, but concludes that, in the present, “los nubelistas no temen a los sindicatos poderosos porque los proletarios de la nube son demasiado débiles para crear uno y los siervos de la nube ni siquiera se consideran productores” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 154)</2>. The structural consequence is that the mechanism through which strong unions converted social power into regulatory capacity is interrupted, rendering the typical tools of social democracy innocuous and shifting the conflict to a terrain in which the prior disarticulation of the class, between the precarization of wage labor and the invisibilization of free labor, prevents collective pressure from stabilizing as a durable political force. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis argues that the classic regulatory grammar of social democracy misses the target in technofeudalism because it takes price as the pressure point in a scenario in which domination is organized precisely outside it, given that the offer to the consumer is frequently presented as “free” or as the cheapest available, while the decisive extraction occurs in the form of rent and access tolls, charged to those who depend on the fief to reach users, circulate goods or simply exist in the digital infrastructure. In this sense he states directly that “La regulación de precios es irrelevante cuando los servicios que el consumidor necesita que se protejan ya son gratuitos o los más baratos del mercado” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 155)</2>, shifting the critique to the architecture of dependence and channel capture, where power is not measured by the margin at the counter, but by the capacity to condition access, visibility and participation through a recurring rent. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis suggests that the antitrust repertoire inherited from the era of “terrestrial” capital loses traction in technofeudalism because it presupposed material and separable objects, whose division was politically difficult, but technically relatively straightforward. In the classic example offered by the author, “Standard Oil“ (a trust famously dissolved by the US Supreme Court in 1911) could be sliced into regional units because its structure presented itself as a set of distributed assets and operations, susceptible to segmentation without altering the nature of what was sold. With cloud capital, however, the core of power is the integration between infrastructure, data and algorithms, so that “dividing” ceases to be merely a legal decision and becomes a technical-political problem about how to separate networks, identities, interoperability standards and command systems without recreating, by another route, the same fief. It is this passage from a “simple” divisibility to a functional indivisibility that he condenses in the question: “Pero ¿cómo se dividirían ahora Amazon, Facebook, PayPal o Tesla?” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 155)</2>, immediately articulated with the idea that domination is also maintained through blocking and retention mechanisms that make exit costly, which helps explain why the traditional threat of “breaking up monopolies” no longer operates as an automatic counterweight. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis formulates the thesis head-on by maintaining that, once technofeudalism is consolidated, the political engineering typical of social democracy loses its point of support, because the social configuration that allowed the State to arbitrate between “capital” and “labor” through strong unions, price regulation and antitrust discipline no longer exists. He condenses this in the diagnosis that “En este nuevo escenario político, la socialdemocracia es imposible”, explaining that “Ya no tenemos al capital en un bando y a los trabajadores en otro, lo que permitiría a un gobierno socialdemócrata hacer de árbitro y obligar a ambas partes a llegar a un acuerdo.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 157)</2>. In place of this polarity, the author describes a board reorganized by the rise of the nubelistas, in which “tenemos un centro y una derecha alternativa, ambos esclavizados por una nueva clase dominante, los nubelistas”, while “la izquierda está absorta en una guerra civil” around internal disputes that do not confront the new regime of command and extraction <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 157)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Varoufakis argues that, in the new political scenario, an important part of “progressive” energy can operate as an escape valve compatible with the preservation of the essential, insofar as authorities manage to perform social liberalism without confronting the material core of technofeudalism. He formulates this by observing that the impulse to protect minorities and to adopt a grammar of restorative justice “le viene muy bien a las personas en el poder que quieren parecer socialmente liberales”, provided that this commitment is above all rhetorical and does not entail “hacer muy poco por proteger a las minorías de las causas sistémicas de su opresión.” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 156- 157)</2>. It is at this point that the argument connects directly to his thesis on cloud capital, because discursive adherence to identity politics functions as a substitute for an economic agenda of confrontation, since “esta adhesión discursiva a la política de la identidad permite a quienes tienen autoridad no hacer nada contra el poder extractivo económico y político que se entrelaza cada vez más con el capital en la nube.” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 157)</4>. The structural effect is a redistributive paralysis directed against the new elite, while the dynamic still feeds the opposing camp, since, as he immediately adds, “a la derecha alternativa, nada podría gustarle más.” <5>Varoufakis</5><6>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 157)</6>. <7>↩</7>

Varoufakis identifies interoperability as the truly sensitive point of the technofief because it attacks the mechanism that makes dependence rational and extraction stable, which is the exit cost produced by the retention of the user's collections and digital life. Comparing it with the telecommunications regulation that imposed interoperability and portability, he states categorically that “Lo único que temen los nubelistas es la interoperabilidad en la nube” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 284)</2>, understood as the possibility of “permitir a sus usuarios pasarse a otro feudo en la nube sin perder sus datos, libros electrónicos, historiales de chat, fotos, música, etcétera” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 284)</4>. The target of the argument is clear: if migration can occur without loss of history and archive, the platform can no longer treat these goods as what keeps the user trapped and, with that, the toll that sustains cloud rent and the power of command associated with the digital enclave diminishes, even though the author himself observes that the technical complexity of this transfer helps explain why the nubelistas “no están preocupados” about the practical imposition of this measure <5>Varoufakis</5><6>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 284)</6>. <7>↩</7>

In Marx, the asymmetry is founded on the separation and control of the objective conditions of labor, which make domination economically “mute” and structural; in Varoufakis, this logic is re-enacted in an environment in which the decisive conditions are not only physical means of production, but privatized infrastructures of mediation that govern access and circulation and convert dependence into a permanent regime of permanence and visibility. The Marxian reference delimits its structural starting point in the asymmetry between those who control the objective conditions of participation in economic life and those who depend on this control to exist economically. In “O Capital” (Book I), Marx formulates the question directly by indicating that the capitalist relation “presupposes the separation between the workers and the ownership of the conditions for the realization of labor” and that, once established, it “not only preserves this separation, but reproduces it on an ever-increasing scale” ([2013], p. 961). Therefore, “the process that creates the capital relation” is precisely the process of separation that “transforms the social means of subsistence and production into capital” and, on the other side, “converts the direct producers into wage workers” ([2013], p. 961). The normative center of this description is that domination need not present itself as permanent direct violence. It stabilizes itself as structural dependence, given that the subject is “free” on the legal-formal plane, but materially compelled to adhere to the conditions imposed by those who control the means. This passage helps sustain the idea that subordination can operate through mediations that dispense with the “whip”. Marx condenses this in the formula of “mute compulsion”: “the mute compulsion exercised by economic relations seals the domination of the capitalist over the worker” ([2013], p. 983); and, although extra-economic violence “continue [...] to be employed”, it appears “only exceptionally”, since “for the usual course of things” it suffices to entrust the worker to the “natural laws of production”, that is, to the “dependence in which he himself finds himself in relation to capital” ([2013], p. 984). What matters to the argument is that, from this perspective, domination derives from differential control of the conditions of access to the social process of production and circulation, and not only from personified coercion or explicit command. It is on the plane of control of conditions and of structural dependence that Varoufakis's reading can be inserted as an update by infrastructural displacement. In technofeudalism, asymmetry is not concentrated only in the factory and in the wage contract, but in private ownership of digital infrastructures that define the economic “right of passage”: platforms function as means of access, circulation and visibility. Hence, for Varoufakis <1>(2024, p. 154)</1>, the nubelistas do not fear unions because “los proletarios de la nube son demasiado débiles para crear uno y los siervos de la nube ni siquiera se consideran productores”, indicating that dependence ceases to be organized primarily as collective wage dependence and comes to be experienced as individualized adherence to systems of mediation. More decisive still, he describes dependence as vulnerability of permanence and of traffic: “Todo capitalista vasallo sabe que si se elimina un enlace de su sitio en la nube podría perder el acceso a la mayor parte de sus clientes […] podrían desaparecer por completo del mundo online”, and concludes that “el tecnofeudalismo se fundamenta en un tecnoterror aséptico”. In this framework, the Marxian “mute compulsion” reappears in the form of an infrastructural coercion: not necessarily physical violence or explicit command, but a continuous threat of de-indexing, de-ranking, banning and loss of network — that is, loss of visibility, reputation and access to the circuits of circulation. <2>↩</2>

Varoufakis links the escalation of inequality to a reordering of classes produced by the concentration of cloud capital, presented synthetically at the very opening of the book, when he states that “los nuevos señores feudales son los propietarios de lo que llama ‘capital de la nube’” and that “los demás hemos vuelto a ser siervos, como en el medievo”, concluding that “Es este nuevo sistema de explotación lo que está detrás del aumento de la desigualdad” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 3)</2>. This seigneurial image does not operate merely as a metaphor, because the preface itself translates the hierarchy into structural dependencies: “real power” ceases to lie with the owners of traditional capital, who “se han convertido en vasallos de una nueva clase de señor feudal, los propietarios del capital en la nube”, while “el resto” returns to the condition of serfs who “contribuimos a la riqueza y el poder de la nueva clase dominante con nuestro trabajo no remunerado” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 8)</4>. The chain closes the bridge between inequality and technofeudalism: when access to digital infrastructures and to channels of circulation becomes the point of command, accumulation shifts to those who control this capital and lowers the others to positions of vassalage and serfdom, which helps explain why the increase in wealth at the top appears as a systemic effect, and not as a conjunctural deviation <5>Varoufakis</5><6>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 3; p. 8)</6>. <7>↩</7>

Varoufakis qualifies the diagnosis of post-2008 inequality by insisting that it was not a simple differential acceleration of gains at the top, but a real impoverishment at the bottom combined with accumulation at the top, which gives inequality a specific regressive meaning in the recent period. He formulates the distinction clearly when he recalls that, “En todas las eras doradas del capitalismo ha aumentado la desigualdad, porque los ricos obtienen beneficios con mayor rapidez que los pobres”, but that “Los años posteriores a 2008 fueron diferentes”, because “La desigualdad no aumentó porque los ingresos de los pobres aumentaran con mayor lentitud que los de los ricos, sino porque sus ingresos disminuyeron en realidad, mientras los financieros y las grandes empresas acumulaban ganancias” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 88)</2>. This nuance connects to the argument about the dissociation between accumulation and profit in the same historical cycle, in which, although profit continues as a subjective horizon, “El beneficio siguió siendo la ambición de todo capitalista, el objetivo de cualquier vendedor”, the effective dynamic changes when “la acumulación de capital […] se desvinculó de los beneficios”, shifting the axis of social prosperity to mechanisms of valorization and capture that do not depend on generalized material improvement <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 93)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Varoufakis links democratic erosion to the erosion of the subject itself by maintaining that cloud capital not only reorganizes markets and rents, but reconfigures the form of individuation, because it shifts identity into an aggregate of behavioral records susceptible to algorithmic modulation. In the author's formulation, technofeudalism radicalizes the psychic effects of “possessive individualism” by knocking down the “enclosure” that still offered the liberal individual some refuge from the market, so that “El capital en la nube ha descompuesto al individuo en fragmentos de datos, una identidad compuesta de elecciones expresadas por clics que sus algoritmos son capaces de manipular”, producing subjects who “más que ser posesivos, están poseídos, personas incapaces de ser dueñas de sí mismas” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 152)</2>. The consequence is that autonomy and self-government cease to be practical presuppositions, since the sphere in which the individual recognized themselves as author of themselves comes to be mediated by devices and platforms that transform choices into raw material for prediction and targeting, shifting freedom of decision into a regime of behavioral governance sustained by the continuous capture of data. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis refuses to treat online hatred as a mere “excess” correctable by marginal adjustments of moderation, because, in technofeudalism, it acquires an economic function internal to the mode of extraction. In describing intolerance as “compensación emocional” in the face of the frustrations and anxieties produced by the dispute over identity and attention, the author insists that comment moderation and the regulation of hate speech “no pueden parar esto” precisely because it is something “intrínseco al capital en la nube”, insofar as “sus algoritmos optimizan las rentas de la nube, que surgen más abundantemente del odio y la insatisfacción” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 153)</2>. The consequence, for the reading of the political economy of the immaterial object of consumption, is that the platform not only tolerates negativity as a flaw to be eliminated, but incorporates it as an input of algorithmic performance, exploiting the attention that becomes fixed through friction, resentment and conflict and converting this fixation into more rent, which shifts the response from the moral plane (good practices of civility) to the structural plane (the design of the circuit of capture and monetization of attention). <3>↩</3>

In closing the geopolitical analysis, Varoufakis formulates a deliberately uncomfortable paradox: after weighing the possibility that “Xi” (referring to Xi Jinping, president of the People's Republic of China) is, at least “en teoría, y de forma muy indirecta”, imposing political limits on the nubelistas and even on Chinese capitalists, but admitting that it is “imposible saberlo” and that not even an eventual wage increase would allow one to conclude that the demos has been revitalized, he concludes that “es muy fascinante que el único rayo de esperanza para cualquier demos del mundo surja en medio de una sociedad sometida al totalitarismo” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 149)</2>. The provocation functions as an indirect critique of the West's regulatory impotence, because it shifts the focus from liberal “good will” to the harder question of the effective capacity to impose brakes on cloud capital, in a scenario in which the political engineering typical of social democracy no longer finds a basis to arbitrate conflicts and “la socialdemocracia es imposible” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 178)</4>. <5>↩</5>

In the appendix in which Varoufakis fixes the vocabulary of political economy that will sustain the comparison between capitalism and technofeudalism, he records that markets “pueden ser más o menos competitivos” and may also assume asymmetries on the demand side, being “oligopsonísticos (muchos vendedores, pocos compradores)” and, at the limit, tending “al monopsonio”, in contrast with asymmetries on the supply side (oligopoly/monopoly) <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 182)</2>. By explicitly inserting the category of oligopsony/monopsony into the very definition of market, he establishes that not every market failure is a “seller's monopoly”, and prepares the next step of the argument, which is to separate these internal distortions of the market from what he calls technofeudalism, in which trade ceases to be a decentralized encounter and comes to be centralized in cloud fiefs run by algorithms that connect the parties under proprietary control <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 182)</4>. <5>↩</5>

In this context, “monopsony” designates the market structure in which there is a single relevant buyer of a good, service or labor, so that demand is concentrated and this buyer manages to influence price, hiring conditions and access rules. “Oligopsony”, in turn, is the variation in which there are few relevant buyers, in a concentration that still allows significant purchasing power, with influence over prices and conditions, including through effects of implicit coordination, standardization of practices or the simple lack of alternatives for those who sell. <1>↩</1>

In the same effort of conceptual systematization in the appendix, Varoufakis turns the lens to the labor market and shows that asymmetry on the demand side also produces appropriation of surplus. He observes that, the greater the competition among employers, the more the wage tends to reflect the exchange value of the worker's commodified labor, but that, “en los mercados laborales dominados por uno o pocos empleadores”, the wage falls below this value and the difference “se traduce en un tipo de renta de monopsonio [...] que se queda el empresario” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 186)</2>. The analytical consequence is that, even within the classic categories of capitalism, rent does not appear only as an “external” or residual phenomenon, but as a structural effect of market power, and this prepares the ground for the book's turn toward rent as the dominant logic when access to cloud fiefs becomes the point of capture. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis uses the comparison to mark that the problem of fief-platforms is not merely “more power” within a market, but the suppression of the very minimal space of economic sociability that still exists even when the market is bad. In “Jeff's world”, Amazon “no es un pueblo con mercado” and “ni siquiera es una especie de mercado digital hipercapitalista”, because “incluso los peores mercados son lugares de encuentro” in which people can still “interactuar e intercambiar información”, and, even under monopoly, “al menos, los compradores pueden hablar entre sí, formar asociaciones, tal vez organizar un boicot de consumo para obligar al monopolista a reducir el precio o mejorar la calidad”; in the fief, by contrast, “todo y todos están intermediados” by an algorithm that does not operate as a “mano invisible”, but as a proprietary mediation that blocks autonomous communication and makes horizontal coordination simply not happen <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 77-78)</2>. This loss of the “commons” is the decisive institutional consequence, because the same technical design that isolates and individualizes the user's experience is what concentrates at the center of the platform the power to bring the parties together or keep them apart, converting a potentially contestable arena into a private domain governed by algorithmic rules. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis describes the passage from recommendation to governance as a shift in the scale and function of the system, in which personalization ceases to be mere convenience and becomes a capacity for command. In the passage in which he follows the daily life of a user with Alexa, he insists that the device “escucha, observa y aprende” preferences and habits and, precisely for this reason, as it “nos va conociendo”, the network operating behind the device “ha adquirido un poder considerable para dirigir nuestra realidad y guiar nuestras elecciones, es decir, para mandar sobre nosotros” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 60)</2>. The consequence, for the central argument, is that cloud-mediated immaterial consumption is not limited to offering or suggesting goods and content, but reorganizes the very experience of the world from an infrastructure that filters, orders and anticipates options, converting the “assistance” interface into a continuous mechanism of behavioral guidance, whose informational asymmetry makes individual resistance a structural problem and not merely a matter of will. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis describes this circuit as a form of recursive capture in which personalization ceases to be merely a reading of preferences and becomes active intervention in the formation of desire. After “getting to know our tastes”, the system comes to “select them” and operates precisely through directed exposure, “exponiéndonos a imágenes, textos y vídeos que elige para condicionar con sutileza nuestros deseos” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 61)</2>. The decisive point is that this architecture does not depend only on surveillance, but on a feedback dynamic in which the user supplies data when interacting and, in doing so, improves the very steering device that repositions them as a target of new stimuli, establishing the “bucle infinito” in which “está entrenándonos para que la entrenemos para que nos entrene para entrenarla para que nos entrene […] ad infinitum” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 61)</4>. The structural consequence, for the argument, is that the immaterial object consumed on the platform already comes coupled to a regime of algorithmic curation that simultaneously records and manufactures dispositions, converting the experience of choice into a sequence of micro-adjustments that reinforces dependence on the channel and expands the commanding capacity of cloud capital. <5>↩</5>

Internal currency as an instrument of administered inflation. Riot admits that it may “sometimes” “alter the purchasing power of the Game Currency” and makes the mechanism explicit: “we may increase the number of Game Currency required to purchase Virtual Products, such as skins” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. At the same time, it states that “we may adjust the prices of any part of the Riot Services at any time (with future effect, that is, with the exception of what you have already acquired)” and that it may “modify, alter or supplement our values and billing methods with future effects”, effective “immediately upon publication” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>. <5>Riot Games</5><6>(Riot Games, 2024e)</6> <7>↩</7>

Denial of the collection's value as an immunization technique. In the same block in which it describes repricing and internal currency, Riot declares: “We do not provide or guarantee, and we expressly deny, any value, in money or otherwise, attributed to any data residing on the servers we operate or control, including any Game Content or Virtual Content attributed to your account” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. The clause is relevant because it attempts to collapse, by definition, what in practice operates as an accumulated immaterial estate. If the contract denies value to the collection, the impoverishment of purchasing power and the deterioration of equivalence tend to be described as a simple dynamic of the service, and not as a legally relevant loss <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>. <5>↩</5>

In the same set of provisions on Virtual Content, Riot reserves for itself a broad power of unilateral intervention over what exists within the fief, including over what the user perceives as a “collection”. The clause is technofeudal not because it suggests mere technical management of the service, but because it assumes asymmetry as the rule: the territory is administered by the lord, the collection is administered by the lord, and the continuity of the value attributed to what has been accumulated depends, ultimately, on the administrative will of whoever controls the infrastructure. <1>↩</1>

In a disclaimer of warranty, Riot states: “The Riot Services are provided to you ‘as is’ and ‘as available’, without warranties or representations of any kind” and adds: “You assume full responsibility for your use of the Riot Services” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. Next, in a limitation of liability, it records that “our total liability to you […] is limited to the total amounts paid by you to Riot during the 12 (twelve) months immediately preceding the time your cause of action arose” and that it is not liable for “business losses” or for “any loss that was not foreseeable [...] (including all indirect damages)”, with the proviso that it does not exclude or limit liability when “it would be unlawful to do so” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>. <5>↩</5>

To clarify the concepts of the argument, the thesis draws on the work of the economist Hal R. Varian. Doctor of Economics from the <1>University of California</1> (Berkeley), Hal R. Varian is a professor, researcher and economist recognized for his contribution to microeconomics and the economics of information. His work helps to fix in a technical-economic sense the notion of price makers employed here. In particular, the work <2>Intermediate Microeconomics: A Modern Approach</2> serves as the basis from which this note draws the distinctions between price-taking firm and price-making firm, as well as correlated categories of market power and mechanisms of price formation. In microeconomics, the basic distinction between competition and market power can be expressed by the difference between the agent who takes price as given and the agent who forms it. In the first case, the producer operates as a price taker, accepting price as an exogenous parameter and concentrating its decision on how much to produce <3>Varian</3><4>(Varian, 2010, p. 397)</4>. In the second case, there is a capacity to influence prices through control of the quantities supplied or demanded, which includes market power on the demand side, as occurs when the monopsonist behaves as a price maker <5>Varian</5><6>(Varian, 2010, p. 489)</6>. The analytical basis of this condition, in the limiting case of a single firm in the market, is that the demand faced by the firm coincides with market demand itself <7>Varian</7><8>(Varian, 2010, p. 396)</8>. Furthermore, a monopolistic structure, in the economic sense relevant to the analysis of market power, assumes that each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve for its product <9>Varian</9><10>(Varian, 2010, p. 478)</10>. Taken together, these premises indicate that the firm with market power does not operate under a given price, but chooses a point on a demand curve, with direct implications for price and quantity. This structure makes it possible to formalize that the price charged can depart from marginal cost in the form of a markup, whose size depends on demand conditions, in particular on elasticity <11>Varian</11><12>(Varian, 2010, p. 443)</12>. In conceptual terms, the elasticity of demand functions as an economic brake on price formation, because the more sensitive the consumer is to price variations, the lower the capacity to sustain increases without relevant loss of quantity. For this reason, conditions that reduce effective substitution and increase switching costs tend to make demand less elastic and, with that, expand the feasible markup, shifting market power from the merely descriptive plane to a mechanism of surplus extraction through pricing. Within this frame, certain structural conditions and market instruments tend to reinforce the capacity for price formation. Barriers to entry, such as licenses and legal restrictions, limit the entry of new competitors, reduce contestability and mitigate competitive pressure even in the face of profit opportunities <13>Varian</13><14>(Varian, 2010, p. 416)</14>. Switching costs can become substantial when components function as systems and the replacement of one element requires replacing others, raising the cost of switching <15>Varian</15><16>(Varian, 2010, p. 674)</16>. When these costs are very high, lock-in (<17>lock-in</17>) can occur, a situation in which switching becomes virtually inconceivable, which is unfavorable to the consumer and, at the same time, attractive to the seller; in this condition, the demand of the locked-in user tends to be very inelastic, allowing the seller to raise prices to extract consumer surplus <18>Varian</18><19>(Varian, 2010, p. 674-675)</19>. Price discrimination strategies consist of selling units of the same product at different prices <20>Varian</20><21>(Varian, 2010, p. 462)</21>, and may assume different degrees according to market segmentation and the form of price differentiation between persons or between quantities purchased <22>Varian</22><23>(Varian, 2010, p. 462)</23>. Bundling (<24>bundling</24>) is part of this repertoire, consisting of the joint offer of related goods in a single package <25>Varian</25><26>(Varian, 2010, p. 474)</26> and reducing the dispersion in willingness to pay, which may allow a higher price to be set for the set <27>Varian</27><28>(Varian, 2010, p. 474)</28>. Segmentation by quality can be operationalized through the deliberate reduction of the quality offered to the lower segment of the market, as a way of inducing self-selection and avoiding cannibalization of sales in the upper segment <29>Varian</29><30>(Varian, 2010, p. 467)</30>. Finally, search costs and costs of acquiring information can generate informational asymmetry and contribute to inefficient outcomes of adverse selection, as when low-quality items drive out high-quality ones because of the high cost of acquiring information <31>Varian</31><32>(Varian, 2010, p. 722)</32>. Taken together, these elements compose a framework in which price formation is not a mere abstract freedom to choose values, but a function of market structure, of the elasticity of demand, of substitution frictions and of the instruments of segmentation and surplus capture. <33>↩</33>

The centrality of the geopolitical dimension is signaled in the very architecture of the book, when Varoufakis devotes an entire chapter to framing Sino-American rivalry as an expression of the technofeudal regime, titling it directly “El impacto global del tecnofeudalismo: la nueva guerra fría” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 126)</2>. In choosing this heading, he does not treat the “new cold war” as a backdrop external to the economic diagnosis, but as one of its modes of manifestation, that is, as a conflict organized around the control of cloud infrastructures and ecosystems and of the forms of dependence they produce.
