The author establishes a true bridge between the internal mutation of capitalism and international politics, making it possible to read state measures and technological disputes as part of the same arrangement of command and extraction that, in the previous chapters, had already displaced markets and profits in favor of fiefs and rent. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis shifts the explanation of the intensification of the Sino-American confrontation from the “geographic” or merely state register to a register of political economy, suggesting that the rhetoric of “seguridad nacional” functions as a veneer for a dispute between technofeudal elites for command over infrastructures and for the preservation of systemic advantages. He makes this point explicit by stating that, “comparada con la Guerra Fría original, la nueva guerra fría tiene poco que ver con la política; está motivada por crudos intereses de clase tecnofeudales” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 135)</2>. The passage ties this motivation to the threat that the advance of Chinese “finanzas en la nube” would represent for the American poles of power, that is, for Wall Street and Silicon Valley, insofar as it would shift the “ventajas comparativas” of the previous arrangement toward the Chinese ruling class <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 135)</4>. Thus, the conflict appears less as a repetition of an ideological antagonism and more as an attempt to prevent a reconfiguration of infrastructural hegemony, in which the capacity to extract and command via the cloud becomes the decisive object of the rivalry. <5>↩</5>

Varoufakis describes the geopolitical bifurcation as a reorganization of the world's digital space into two blocs of command, in which rivalry does not operate only through tariffs, military alliances or classic “territorial” disputes, but through the consolidation of cloud infrastructures that function as domains of access and extraction. The author states that, under the combined impact of the war in Ukraine and the “gran inflación”, in an environment that “están empeorando la pobreza, agravando el cambio climático y generando una atmósfera de miedo”, “el mundo se está dividiendo en dos superfeudos en la nube antagónicos: uno estadounidense, el otro chino”, and that “no saldrá nada bueno y valioso de esta bifurcación” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 141)</2>. Read in continuity with the diagnosis that the new cold war is driven by “crudos intereses de clase tecnofeudales” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 135)</4>, this division into superfiefs appears as the geopolitical translation of platform power on a planetary scale, converting the dispute between States into a dispute over hegemonic digital ecosystems that condition dependencies, alignments and margins of autonomy outside the traditional terrain of market competition. <5>↩</5>

Varoufakis treats the freezing of Russian reserves as a turning point in the international monetary architecture because it makes visible, inescapably, that dollar hegemony is not merely a “market fact”, but a power of political blockade exercisable over sovereign wealth. The invasion of Ukraine functions as the trigger for a response that “cambió toda la ecuación”, when “la Reserva Federal congeló cientos de miles de millones de dólares que pertenecían al banco central ruso”, keeping them “dentro del circuito de pagos en dólares que Estados Unidos controla por completo” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 136)</2>. The consequence, for the author, is a systemic signal sent to the rest of the major holders of dollar assets, since “fue la primera vez en la historia capitalista que el dinero de un banco central importante era confiscado por otro banco central” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 136)</4>, making the search for alternative routes of settlement and reserve more rational and, in this way, contributing to the acceleration of the cleavage he describes as the division of the world into “dos superfeudos en la nube antagónicos” <5>Varoufakis</5><6>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 141)</6>. In presenting the digital yuan, Varoufakis frames it as an infrastructural response to dependence on the dollarized payments circuit and, therefore, as a piece of monetary-technological sovereignty on the technofeudal board. In the didactic example, the author contrasts the friction of “conventional” international transfers with the hypothesis of People's Bank of China wallets, in which the remittance is completed “al instante y sin coste alguno”, precisely because settlement in digital yuan eliminates cascading intermediaries and, above all, bypasses “el canal internacional de transferencia de dinero que está totalmente controlado por las autoridades estadounidenses” <7>Varoufakis</7><8>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 138)</8>. The political consequence of the design is explicit, since, by reducing the need to pass through banks, central banks and the dollarized corridor, the digital yuan appears as “la peor pesadilla de Washington y los banqueros privados” <9>Varoufakis</9><10>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 139)</10>, that is, as a direct threat to the capacity for control exercised by the US over flows and sanctions within the payments system. <11>↩</11>

In projecting the “new cold war” as a dispute between cloud infrastructures, Varoufakis suggests that it reduces third parties to a geopolitics of dependence, in which autonomy becomes a function of access to cloud capital and to the circuits that sustain it. In the European case, vulnerability does not stem only from diplomatic decisions, but from a material lack of its own capacity in the new regime, so that “La falta de capital en la nube de Europa significa que la nueva guerra fría, sumada a la crisis energética provocada por la guerra en Ucrania que afectó a sus fabricantes, ya han hecho que Europa sea geoestratégicamente irrelevante” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 143)</2>. For the Global South, the bifurcation appears as a forced choice between competing digital domains, because “Con el mundo dividido en dos superfeudos en la nube, uno basado en el dólar y el otro en el yuan, se ven obligados a elegir un señor feudal al que someterse” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 143)</4>, and this pressure intensifies when the old arrangement of financial circulation closes, since “La nueva crisis de deuda está obligando a las clases dirigentes del sur global a elegir un bando” <5>Varoufakis</5><6>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 144)</6>. The structural consequence of the argument is that US-China rivalry tends to translate, for Europeans and peripheral countries, into compulsory alignment with standards, payment channels and data ecosystems they do not control, with increased vulnerability to blockades, access conditions and tolls imposed by the respective “superfiefs”. <7>↩</7>

Varoufakis makes explicit that to “exit” technofeudalism is not equivalent to adjusting incentives or correcting regulatory excesses, because the core of the problem lies in the property relations that structure social life itself as mediated by the cloud. In linking his critique to the “death of the liberal individual”, he maintains that recovering freedom as individual sovereignty requires a change of architecture, since “rescatar esa idea liberal fundacional —la libertad como soberanía individual— exigirá, por lo tanto, una reconfiguración completa de los derechos de propiedad sobre los instrumentos de producción, distribución, colaboración y comunicación, que cada vez se basan más en la nube” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 153)</2>. The consequence is avowedly disruptive, since, to reconstitute the liberal subject under technofeudal conditions, “tenemos que hacer algo que los liberales detestan: planear una nueva revolución” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 153)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Varoufakis describes “democratized companies” as an arrangement in which shareholding ceases to be a tradable asset and becomes inalienable political membership, because the corporate bond merges with the employment bond. The legal form is purposely simple and egalitarian: “cada empleado tiene una única acción que recibe al ser contratado”, a share that “no se puede vender ni alquilar” and that “otorga a cada empleado un único voto” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 165)</2>. With this, decision-making power ceases to be a prerogative of share capital and is redistributed as everyday governance, since “todas las decisiones […] se adoptan de manera colectiva” and the vote is exercised through the intranet, conceived as “una asamblea permanente de accionistas” <3>Varoufakis</3><4>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 165)</4>. The intended institutional effect is to cut the typical mediation of finance and speculation, because the rule of “sólo una” non-tradable share per employee both dissolves the figure of the external shareholder and reconfigures the company as a space of deliberation and not as an object of purchase and sale <5>Varoufakis</5><6>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 165)</6>. <7>↩</7>

Varoufakis inserts the governance of land into his “technodemocracy” as a way of inverting the political meaning of ground rent, converting it from a mechanism of private capture into a tool of collective provision. The institutional design is local and deliberately oriented toward redistribution, since “cada región está gestionada por una Asociación Municipal” charged with “supervisa[r] la división del suelo entre zonas comerciales y sociales”, so that “las rentas recaudadas en las primeras financian la provisión de viviendas sociales en las segundas” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 173)</2>. The question is not merely to regulate the real estate market, but to redesign the circuit through which territory produces dependence, making ground rent a stable funding base for social housing and, with that, removing from housing the role of everyday axis of economic subjection. <3>↩</3>

Varoufakis frames the proposal as an exchange of infrastructure to dismantle the technofeudal model grounded in the “deception” of gratuity, replacing it with an arrangement in which data cease to be extracted by default and come to circulate under express and paid authorization. The alternative appears as a “plataforma de micropagos”, which he calls “Un céntimo por tus pensamientos”, combined with a “Carta de Derechos Digitales” that “garantiza a todo el mundo el derecho a elegir qué datos vender y a quién”, so that “los desarrolladores de aplicaciones que necesitan nuestros datos tienen que pagar para obtener los de los usuarios que den su consentimiento” <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 168)</2>. The institutional consequence is to reposition the user from object of capture to holder of decision, shifting the axis of the system from attention and involuntary tracking to a regime of priced consent and, with that, attacking the typical form of cloud rent that feeds on informational asymmetry and on the lock-in produced by the appearance of a “free” service. <3>↩</3>

Under the structure of the hypothesis on which the logical path of this discussion is built, informational rentierism is treated as a way of organizing consumption in platform environments, and not merely as a macroeconomic diagnosis. In Dowbor<1><2>192</2></1>, the focus shifts from the image of the fief to the toll economy and to the demand monopoly, that is, to the control of circuits of access, visibility and transaction that converts connectivity into <3>p. 184</3> recurring rent. This lens makes it possible to reconstruct, in consumerist language, why the protection of the CDC cannot be limited to the initial delivery, or even to a single moment of supply, since the utility of the IOC depends on continued governance and on conditions whose auditability is structurally asymmetric.

The analysis of platform capitalism, from the perspective of Ladislau Dowbor, requires recognizing a structural inflection in the regime of accumulation that is not to be confused with a mere technological update of the industrial paradigm. Dowbor describes the consolidation of a “new mode of production” and informational accumulation<1><2>193</2></1>, in which the axis of social command shifts from physical manufacture to the strategic governance of intangible assets, of financialization and of technology. In his historical typology, the modern digital economy not only instrumentalizes information, but converts it into the most valuable resource of the regime of accumulation, instituting a pattern of appropriation that operates above the level of the effective producer and repositions the bases of a private economic sovereignty, understood as the capacity to define rules of access, extraction and monetization through infrastructures controlled by private agents.

Dowbor's interpretive key matters here because it reconstructs, at the micro level, what is often naturalized as an update routine or mere “evolution of the service”. In platform ecosystems, the utility of the immaterial good depends on recognition, visibility and permanence governed by the supplier itself, so that unilateral changes are not lateral noise, but an instrument of capture. The relevant asymmetry is not only informational. It is infrastructural, because it makes it possible to impose frictions, urgencies and calibrated losses that convert permanence into an economic condition of consumption, as observed in the empirical laboratory <1>Riot Games</1>.

In this shift, platform capitalism is characterized by the action of digital structures that operate as demand monopolies<1><2>194</2></1>, capable of extracting rent through concentrated and asymmetric control of informational flows, beyond the classic logic of the one-off sale of commodities. “The result is the so-called ‘demand monopolies’: <3>p. 185</3> we have to use what others use, because without it we do not communicate, besides the fact that they buy any competitor that tries to open up space” <4>Dowbor</4><5>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24)</5>. The generation of value comes to depend, primarily, on the control of interfaces, data and sign systems, that is, of the semiotically mediated material conditions that organize access, guide decision and modulate the very experience of the consumer's enjoyment.

In the scope adopted here, “informational rentierism” in Dowbor can be defined as the contemporary form of appropriation of surplus that stabilizes itself not through the proportional production of goods and services, but through the strategic administration of rights of passage over vital flows of economic and social life. It is a regime in which value is extracted through the capacity to organize and govern access to information-dense circuits, such as communication, payment, circulation of content, intermediations and decisions, converting connectivity itself into a recurring source of rent. The core of command thus shifts from the domain of manufacture to the capture of the process, since whoever controls the platform controls the points of entry and permanence and can transform each crossing into a toll <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 13; p. 20; p. 51-52)</2>.

This shift, matured over recent decades, reorganized the core of the system, since accumulation ceased to rest primarily on the production and circulation of goods and came to be structured in mechanisms of rent extraction grounded in the control of intangible assets, especially data, platforms and intellectual property regimes. It is within this horizon that Dowbor uses the term “toll economy”<1><2>195</2></1>, that is, the capture of essential flows and of mandatory points of passage, in which value is appropriated through control of access, intermediations and circuits of circulation on an increasing scale, in clear mismatch with any corresponding increase in social production. “Many services are useful, or even necessary, but generate disproportionate profits relative to their contribution, as in the case of communication oligopolies. Rentiers earn not so much from the services they provide, as from the obligation for everyone to pass through their turnstiles.” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21)</4>.

In the informational environment, the toll economy is realized with particular effectiveness through legal-technical enclosures, since intellectual property rights, <1>p. 186</1> license agreements, account architecture and access control mechanisms become governance infrastructure and transform access to and permanence in the ecosystem into a recurring source of extraction <2>Dowbor</2><3>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 7; p. 21; p. 41)</3>. The very transit through signs, such as interfaces, reputation, digital inventories, profile identities, currencies and content, comes to be captured as an economically exploitable flow.

The IOC, as the concretization of the immaterial product in the sense of Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC, appears here not as neutral content, but as a commodity form whose enjoyment is subordinated to contractual and technological turnstiles, so that one does not buy merely an item, but the revocable permission to remain within an ecosystem of signs. It is the same legal-technical enclosure that allows the platform to administer internal inflation by controlling the practical unit of account, the conversion mechanisms and the price anchors, shifting the formation of values to a regime of opaque calibration by <1>design</1>, with low comparability and high dependence on permanence.

Rentier capture through governance intensifies the user's vulnerability in the practice of digital consumption, described here as a dimension of factual vulnerability. Inserted into ecosystems of signs whose permanence is conditioned by contractual and technological turnstiles, the consumer is induced by anticipation and by promises of availability, continuity and functionality that they cannot reconstruct in their decisive elements, since delivery is not accompanied by transparency criteria about its limitations and, in practice, is fully and unilaterally modulable by the supplier <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 19-21)</2>.

In this scenario, the very justification of intellectual property tends to operate in an instrumental key, tied to the stimulus of future creations <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>, so that the hypertrophy of duration and scope may produce a mismatch between incentive and blockage. In <3>copyright</3>, the realization of profits tends to be concentrated in the first cycles of exploitation, around five or, at most, ten years after publication, while exclusivity may last for decades, becoming a fence that restricts access <4>Dowbor</4><5>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</5>. For the economic analysis developed here, the decisive point is that intellectual property, when coupled to the platform, ceases to appear merely as an external legal title and comes to operate as a material component of the closure of access, that is, as a functional gear of the toll economy in the informational environment.

The toll economy described by Dowbor is not limited to extraction from end consumers, since it reorganizes the entire chain by subordinating traditional companies to private infrastructures of intermediation and converting the intangible into a general condition of circulation. The social surplus comes to be appropriated less through production and more through the <1>p. 187</1> capacity to impose rights of passage over activities and flows already socially produced, on a planetary scale, without proportional counterpart in goods, services or jobs. For this reason, Dowbor <2>(2024, p. 13)</2> maintains that rentierism appropriates the surplus without corresponding productive contribution. It is precisely this decoupling between contribution and capture that makes enclosure legally sensitive, because, when platforms and titles of exclusivity operate as permanent turnstiles, the rationale of incentive loses descriptive centrality and the problem of access control emerges as an instrument of extraction, with informational asymmetry and operational opacity relevant to consumer protection.

In this toll economy, the dominant mechanism of surplus extraction shifts. It moves away from a productive regime in which accumulation is organized above all through the exploitation of labor and the discipline of production and approaches an arrangement in which capture is structured by financial and communication platforms and by platforms for the appropriation of private data, with the prevalence of rent over productive accumulation<1><2>196</2></1>. The disproportion between effective productive contribution and observed enrichment ceases to indicate a peripheral distortion and comes to point to a qualitative shift in systemic dynamics, in which rentier logic becomes the organizing principle <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8-9; p. 20)</4>. In this direction, profit on production has evolved into rentierism on intermediation <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 68)</6>.

The logic of the toll presents itself in a harsher key when power ceases to operate only through network effects and comes to rest on the control of critical infrastructure of the digital economy. By consolidating services and circuits of computing, logistics and intermediation on which third parties come to depend in order to operate, an infrastructure rentierism is formed, sustained by recurring tolls and by structurally irreplicable barriers to entry, anchored in scale, integration and systemic dependence <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>.

Thus, the shift from productive capitalism to a rentier regime can be described as a break in proportionality between productive contribution and appropriation of surplus. The extraction of value stabilizes itself through position and through control of points of passage, such as networks, infrastructures and intermediations, and not through a correlated increase in social utility, <1>p. 188</1> reorganizing accumulation as a systematic drain on social wealth <2>Dowbor</2><3>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 13; p. 20)</3>.

In the scope adopted here, Dowbor's critique matters above all for the way in which the platform converts access into rent through the control of informational flows and of decisions on visibility, access and permanence. In this movement, intellectual property regimes cease to operate as simple titles of authorship and come to integrate the infrastructure of control, delimiting possibilities of use, circulation and recombination of digital assets. A regime of authorization and blockage is thus sustained, which structures the consumer's experience as a process that is entirely capturable from an economic point of view.

In the informational paradigm, knowledge assumes the position of central factor of production, but its economic logic is not to be confused with that of physical goods, since, unlike material goods, shared knowledge is not lost to the one who shares it, as it is not a rival good and access to it can be generalized <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 11)</2>. This non-rivalry shifts the axis of conflict to the forms of access control, which makes intelligible why immaterial consumer goods and digital experiences, as IOCs, can be technically reproducible and, even so, legally and technically made scarce through regimes of authorization and blockage that organize consumption.

By emphasizing the centrality of knowledge as a factor of production and the platform as the hegemonic form of economic organization, Dowbor suggests that the twenty-first century is structured by an economy in which globalized and digitalized technical infrastructure reconfigures time and space, while the surplus is appropriated by actors capable of managing signals, algorithms and intermediations on a planetary scale. From this follows his diagnosis of a system qualitatively more extractive and unproductive than industrial capitalism, insofar as capture stabilizes itself through control of access and mediations. The decisive point for the present analysis is not to deny the persistence of the productive base, but to show its structural subordination to informational-financial command, which comes to define who accesses the market, through which mediations and under which conditions of subjection <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 27)</2>.

Within this closure typical of demand monopolies, the network is converted into economic coercion and produces structural dependence. The consumer's individual choice is neutralized by the inevitability of the technological standard, so that the platform comes to operate as a coercive infrastructure of everyday life. In this arrangement, the algorithm articulates economic calculation and social modeling, organizing micro-dynamics of capture under decision-making opacity, while human attention is elevated to the category of raw material and absorbed by <1>p. 189</1> an interface <2>design</2> that governs signs, hierarchizes visibilities and maximizes permanence and emotional excitability as economically measurable variables.

From Dowbor's perspective, algorithmic capillarity not only expands scale, but reconfigures the user as a unit treatable by calculation<1><2>197</2></1>, that is, as an individual isolable and governable by inference, converted simultaneously into a source of information, risk and return. Along these lines, the author states that billions of people cease to represent an incalculable mass and become isolable individuals, sources of information and customers, whether they like it or not <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</4>. Within this horizon, the offer ceases to operate as a uniform pattern knowable in advance and comes to function as a contingent set of conditions modulated by continuous segmentation and optimization <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28)</6>. The consumer's experience thus becomes a field of silent adjustments of frictions, permissions and benefits, whose practical effect is the directed instability of the promised functional value, with enough opacity to frustrate auditing and to shift control of enjoyment to the platform.

These silent adjustments of frictions, permissions and benefits rest on the normative and technical reintroduction of scarcity, which does not operate as simple “pricing”, but as a programmed restriction of circulation. Economic freedom is thus preserved for the agent who controls the infrastructure, while costs of freedom and autonomy are transferred to the user, reconfiguring the space of consumption as a zone of dependence and management. The asymmetry is particularly sensitive in IOCs, in which experience, access and rights of use take place under opaque and unilateral mediations, creating conditions for an extractive rationality of value capture through access control.

This reading, however, is not reduced to a denunciation of the technical potential of digitalization, precisely because the scarcity described here is socially imposed and not a given of the nature of the informational. Dowbor insists on the ambivalence of knowledge as an immaterial good, since, not being rival in nature, it can be shared at no additional marginal cost, which opens the objective possibility of collaborative reorganization and of generalization of access to cultural and educational goods. The legal-political problem emerges when rentier capture converts this technical abundance into scarcity, reintroducing artificial barriers and mechanisms <1>p. 190</1> of appropriation to preserve the logic of rent in an environment that would allow the expansion of the commons. It is this tension between emancipatory potential and rentier appropriation that makes the ontological transition described by Dowbor at once a critique of the present and a dispute over the institutional destiny of the digital <2>Dowbor</2><3>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 10-11; p. 42; p. 45)</3>.

The decisive point in Dowbor lies in understanding that digital monetization does not depend only on the sale of commodities, but on the capture of continuous flows of data and payments on a planetary scale and at low granularity, through mechanisms that operate below the user's radar and frequently outside public intelligibility. This diagnosis is condensed in the description of everyday life mediated by platforms and payment systems, which leads the author to conclude that a system of micro-drainage of the resources and personal information of billions of people has been generated<1><2>198</2></1> <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</4>. “Micro-drainage” designates a fractional and repeated extraction, made possible by algorithmic capillarity and by inference technologies that make each individual addressable as an economic target, and operationalized by tracking devices such as cookies and related identifiers.

Monetization, therefore, is not episodic, but permanent, cumulative and automated, converting private information into an asset and connectivity itself into a condition of economic subjection. Beyond the economic aspect, micro-drainage is legally sensitive because it produces an asymmetry of auditability. The platform centralizes and exclusively controls logs, metrics and modulation criteria, such as profiling, ranking and recommendation, while the consumer sees only the interface and its effects. As a result, the problem ceases to be merely one of “cost” and comes to involve evidence and material transparency, since the user has no means to reconstruct the link between capture, processing and consequences in the offer and in the experience.

Dowbor <1>(2024)</1> presents digital rentierism as the central economic vector of the twenty-first century and identifies, at the top of this machinery, platform conglomerates that occupy a dominant position in the organization of markets, in informational circulation and in demand itself. Taking companies such as Google, Amazon and Facebook as examples, he emphasizes that these structures operate as global monopolies capable of capturing surpluses through intermediation, data and access control, and not through a proportional relationship with the traditional production of goods and <2>p. 191</2> services. It is from this position of command that one understands why micro-drainage and the asymmetry of auditability are not accidents of digital consumption, but foreseeable effects of a market architecture founded on opaque intermediations and unilateral modulations. In addressing the subject, Dowbor shifts the focus from individual luxury to the dynamic of reinvestment and expansion of capacities, stating that the point is not to have yachts and airplanes, but to have a company generating profits that will be reinvested in more productive capacities <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 5)</4>. On the distributive plane, the shift is expressed in the rupture between appropriation of surplus and productive contribution and in the drain on social wealth typical of unproductive rentierism, breaking the minimum of proportionality between how much one contributes and how much one becomes rich <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 13; p. 20)</6>. This movement is further articulated with high finance and with investment structures that reinforce the stability and expansive capacity of platform power.
